overview: Orora is an ASX-listed (June fiscal year end) global beverage packaging company operating two standalone segments: Cans (aluminium beverage can manufacturing and decoration across Australia and New Zealand) and Glass (premium glass bottles for spirits, wine and cosmetics via France-headquartered Saverglass, plus Australian glass maker Gawler). The portfolio was reshaped over 2020-2025 through the sale of the Fibre (corrugated/recycling) business to Nippon Paper (FY2020), the debt- and equity-funded acquisition of Saverglass (December 2023, ~A$2.16bn), and the divestment of the North American Packaging Solutions (OPS) business to Veritiv and an Adelaide aluminium closures operation (both completed FY2025), leaving a focused beverage-packaging pure play.

business_model.summary: Orora manufactures and decorates packaging under long-term, largely B2B contracts with beverage, spirits, wine and cosmetics brand owners. Cans revenue includes pass-through aluminium costs with margin earned on conversion/decoration; Glass revenue is driven by bespoke bottle design, decoration and technical capability sold to premium spirits, wine and champagne houses. No single customer exceeds 10% of group revenue, reducing concentration risk, but demand is tied to end-consumer beverage categories (beer, RTD, energy drinks, spirits, wine).
business_model.customer_type: B2B - global and regional beverage, spirits, wine and cosmetics brand owners (FMCG); no customer >10% of group revenue
business_model.geographic_mix: Cans: Australia/New Zealand. Glass: Saverglass manufactures in France (core), with sites in Mexico (Acatlán), UAE (Ras Al Khaimah), and the US (California), selling globally into premium spirits/wine/cosmetics; Gawler is Australia-only.

main_competitors: Visy Industries (Australian glass, near-duopoly with Gawler)
competitive_position.market_position: Leading positions in niche, structurally advantaged segments: a scaled Cans manufacturer in the consolidated Australia/NZ market, and Saverglass as a global leader in premium/super-premium glass bottles for spirits, wine and cosmetics (differentiated from the larger, more commoditised global glass majors O-I, Verallia, Vidrala and Ardagh). Gawler and Visy effectively form a duopoly in Australian container glass.

moat_factors.description: Technical engineering and decoration expertise for premium bottle shapes/finishes creates switching costs with luxury spirits, champagne and cosmetics brands that Orora management describes as a leading global position

moat_factors.factor: Scale and capital intensity in ANZ cans/glass
moat_factors.description: High fixed-cost manufacturing (furnaces, can lines) and a consolidated regional market structure (near-duopoly dynamics with Visy in glass) limit new entrants in Australia/NZ

moat_factors.factor: Long-term customer relationships / low customer concentration
moat_factors.description: No single customer >10% of group revenue; deep, multi-year commercial relationships with beverage brand owners
Cans contracts largely pass through LME aluminium price movements to customers, insulating EBIT from raw material volatility
Saverglass plants across France, Mexico, UAE and the US provide customer proximity and some ability to shift production across regions to mitigate tariffs/disruption

weaknesses: Glass/Saverglass earnings are highly exposed to discretionary premium spirits and wine demand, which has proven more cyclical and slower to recover than assumed at acquisition
Geographic concentration risk crystallised in FY26: the Ras Al Khaimah (UAE) facility was forced into a closed-loop/suspended state by the Middle East conflict
Saverglass is a mid-sized specialist versus much larger, more diversified global glass majors (O-I, Verallia, Ardagh) with greater scale economies
FY26 non-cash impairment of A$742.8m (comprising A$676.4m of Saverglass goodwill) signals the 2023 acquisition was priced on overly optimistic post-COVID demand assumptions
Unfranked dividends and reliance on Conduit Foreign Income Account status reduce the after-tax attractiveness for domestic franking-sensitive investors

growth_drivers: Cans capacity expansion (Revesby second line, Rocklea third line commissioning Q1 FY27) completes a multi-year capex cycle, with no further growth capex required until after 2030 and management guiding ~4-6% long-term volume growth
Structural consumer shift toward aluminium cans and growth in RTD, energy drink and non-alcohol beverage categories supporting Cans volumes
Helio by Orora digital can-printing technology enabling premium, short-run decoration and deeper customer co-development

Glass/Saverglass turnaround plan targeting >€30m of net EBIT run-rate improvement by FY30 via six business priorities (new business wins, speed to market, operational efficiency, overhead reduction, cash generation)

Glass network optimisation largely complete (Le Havre F4 furnace closure, Ghlin furnace modernisation adding ~25% capacity, two-furnace Gawler operation), supporting margin recovery once premium beverage demand normalises
Conservative balance sheet (1.2x EBITDA leverage vs 1.5-2.5x target range) provides capacity for continued capital returns (buybacks/dividends) as Cans capex cycle ends
Lightweighting and sustainability initiatives (recycled content, oxyfuel furnace gas savings) supporting cost efficiency and customer ESG requirements

business.description: Saverglass volumes grew 5.9% in FY26 but revenue/EBIT fell as cost-of-living pressures and slower premiumisation shifted category and within-category mix toward lower-value products, cutting average selling price and margin
The Middle East conflict forced the RAK (UAE) facility into a closed-loop/idled state from April 2026, with only a restricted-volume restart (via Oman ports) planned from October 2026
Alcohol-moderation trends threaten long-term wine/spirits volume growth, though offset by structural RTD/energy drink growth benefiting Cans
Operates in markets with varying barriers to entry; larger global glass majors (O-I, Verallia, Ardagh, Vidrala) and global can makers (Ball, Crown) could pressure pricing/share
A contractor fatality occurred at the Acatlán (Mexico) Saverglass site in July 2026; Lost Time Injury frequency rose in FY26, concentrated at European glass sites

financial.description: FY26 saw a A$742.8m non-cash impairment to the Glass CGU (incl. A$676.4m Saverglass goodwill) after management pushed out its expected earnings-recovery timeline; failure to hit the >€30m FY30 EBIT improvement target could trigger further write-downs
Saverglass earnings are generated in EUR and translated to AUD; EUR/AUD moved from 59.6c to 58.2c in FY26, amplifying the reported EBIT decline

financial.risk: Rising net debt / leveraged capital returns
financial.description: Net debt rose A$226.9m to A$481.1m in FY26 due to buybacks and growth capex, though leverage of 1.2x EBITDA remains below the 1.5-2.5x target range

financial.risk: Elevated payout ratio amid falling earnings
financial.description: FY26 dividend payout ratio was 78% of underlying NPAT (down from 86% in FY25) on declining EPS; dividends are unfranked

regulatory.description: Operations span Australia, France, Mexico, UAE and the US, each with distinct fiscal, environmental and trade regimes
Management cites US tariff actions as compounding demand/margin pressure on customers and on the business directly
FY26 was the first year of mandatory AASB S2 climate disclosures; Gawler is subject to the National Greenhouse and Energy Reporting Safeguard Mechanism

macro.description: The Middle East conflict directly disrupted the RAK facility and Saverglass's regional supply chain in FY26

macro.risk: Global recession / demand weakness in US and China
macro.description: Management flags simultaneous demand weakness in the US and China - two key end-markets for customers - as a risk of a deeper or longer premium-beverage downturn
Aluminium price volatility is largely passed through to Cans customers; energy costs for glass furnaces are partly mitigated by efficiency gains (e.g., G3 oxyfuel furnace, 31% gas reduction)

execution.description: The FY26 impairment reflects a reassessment that Saverglass's earnings recovery, relative to the December 2023 acquisition case (priced partly on post-COVID stimulus-driven demand), will take materially longer than expected

Group CFO Shaun Hughes is departing after six years; incoming CFO Paul Victor (ex Mainland Group, Sasol, Incitec Pivot) joins in FY27, introducing near-term leadership transition risk during the Glass turnaround
Delivering the >€30m FY30 EBIT improvement depends on executing furnace closures/rebuilds (Le Havre, Ghlin), the RAK restart via Oman, and six new commercial priorities simultaneously

macro_factors.industry_outlook: Cans: structurally favourable, supported by the consumer shift to aluminium, RTD and energy-drink growth, and a largely sold-out Australian/NZ capacity base post-expansion. Glass/premium spirits-wine: currently in a cyclical downturn driven by cost-of-living pressures and slower premiumisation following the unwind of post-COVID stimulus-driven demand; management targets recovery and >€30m of EBIT improvement by FY30.
macro_factors.cyclicality: Mixed - Cans is relatively defensive (staple beverage categories, pass-through input costs); Glass/Saverglass is more cyclical and discretionary, tied to premium spirits/wine consumption and consumer confidence.
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: Moderate - net debt of A$481m at 1.2x EBITDA (below the 1.5-2.5x target range); Orora extended debt maturities with a new €210m USPP note issuance (7- and 10-year tranches) and an amended syndicated facility completed 30 June 2026, pushing core refinancing needs out to FY30.
key_input_costs: Aluminium (LME-linked, largely pass-through in Cans contracts)
Glass raw materials (silica sand, soda ash, recycled cullet)

recent_developments.event: FY26 results: revenue (continuing ops) $2,225.9m (+6.5%), EBIT $248.2m (-5.3%), statutory net loss of $616.6m after a $758.8m after-tax significant item, dominated by a $742.8m non-cash Glass impairment (incl. $676.4m Saverglass goodwill); FY26 dividend 9.0cps (78% payout, unfranked)

Trading update: Orora paused its on-market share buyback and cut FY26 Saverglass EBIT guidance, citing disruption from the Middle East conflict; analysts (Jefferies, Citi) cut price targets, with Citi applying a 'High Risk' rating
Ras Al Khaimah (UAE) Saverglass facility suspended production and shifted to a 'closed loop' hot operation after Middle East conflict closed key shipping routes; most staff repatriated
Commenced modernisation/rebuild of the Ghlin (Belgium) glass furnace (~25% capacity increase), commissioning expected early FY27
Completed issuance of new €210m seven- and ten-year USPP notes and amended/extended the syndicated bank facility, extending average debt maturity to ~5.4 years
A contractor fatality occurred in a vehicle-related incident at the Acatlán, Mexico Saverglass site; investigation underway

AGM held (13-14 October); Chair acknowledged shareholder disappointment over the Saverglass impairment and acquisition outcomes; on-market buyback activity resumed/continued under a second program (up to 10% of shares, announced 12 February 2026)
Rocklea (Queensland) third can line nearing commissioning (expected Q1 FY27), completing the multi-year Cans capacity expansion program
CFO Shaun Hughes to depart after six years; incoming Group CFO Paul Victor (ex Mainland Group, Sasol, Incitec Pivot) to join in FY27

items.notes: Driven by benefits of completed capacity expansion (Revesby, Rocklea) and continued volume growth of ~4-6% p.a.

items.target: Expected to be below FY26 level
items.notes: Near-term earnings weighted to H2 FY27; reflects continued soft premium spirits/wine demand and geopolitical disruption

To be delivered via six business priorities: win new business, increase speed to market, enhance operational efficiency, reduce overhead costs, strengthen cash generation, and commercial/pricing initiatives
Supported by capacity now fully built out; no further Cans growth capex required until after 2030
FY26 actual leverage of 1.2x EBITDA sits below the target range, implying balance-sheet capacity for further capital returns

items.target: 60%-80% of underlying NPAT, franked to the extent possible
items.notes: FY26 actual payout was 78%, at the top of the range, on unfranked dividends

guidance.management_commentary: Chair Rob Sindel and CEO Brian Lowe both characterised FY26 as a year of 'divergent' and 'contrasting' performance - strong Cans offsetting weak Glass - and stated the $742.8m impairment does not change the long-term strategic rationale for owning Saverglass but 'does increase the importance of effective execution' of the Glass turnaround plan. Management reiterated that the impairment is non-cash and does not affect FY27 operating cash flow or liquidity, and that the external environment for Glass 'remains uncertain' in the near term.

bull_case: Cans is a structurally advantaged, high-return segment now exiting a multi-year capex cycle (Rocklea completion Q1 FY27), positioning the Group for a step-up in free cash flow as capacity investment ends and utilisation rises

Conservative balance sheet (1.2x EBITDA, below the 1.5-2.5x target range) and extended, well-laddered debt maturities (new €210m USPP notes) give Orora flexibility to keep returning capital via buybacks/dividends even through the Glass downturn

The FY26 Saverglass impairment is non-cash and did not impair FY26 free cash flow or liquidity; a clear, quantified turnaround plan (>€30m net EBIT improvement by FY30) with network optimisation largely complete gives a path to margin recovery if premium spirits/wine demand normalises

Portfolio diversification between defensive Cans (RTD/energy-drink tailwinds) and cyclical premium Glass provides a natural hedge, and the current depressed Glass earnings/valuation may represent a cyclical trough rather than a structural decline

Management has shown a consistent willingness to simplify the portfolio (Fibre, OPS, Closures divestments) and reset expectations, which, combined with a new CFO, could sharpen capital-allocation discipline going forward
bear_case: The Saverglass acquisition (~A$2.16bn, December 2023) has proven value-destructive, with a $742.8m impairment within less than three years raising real doubts about management's underwriting discipline and whether further write-downs are possible if the FY30 recovery targets are missed

Premium spirits and wine end-markets face potentially structural, not just cyclical, headwinds (alcohol moderation, cost-of-living pressure, slower premiumisation) that could keep Saverglass earnings depressed well beyond management's own FY27 guidance of 'below FY26'

Geopolitical and trade disruption (Middle East conflict idling the RAK facility, US tariffs) adds volatility and execution risk precisely in the segment already underperforming, with no clear end date for normalisation

The dividend payout ratio is already at the top of the 60-80% target range (78% FY26) on falling underlying earnings and unfranked distributions, leaving limited headroom if Glass earnings deteriorate further

Analyst sentiment has turned materially more negative post-impairment (Jefferies and Citi price-target cuts, Citi's 'High Risk' rating), reflecting broader skepticism about near-term Glass earnings visibility and management credibility after the writedown
